kurals.tamil:
இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான் இயல்புடைய மூவர்க்கும்
நல்லாற்றின் நின்ற துணை.
kurals.transliteration:
Ilvaazhvaan enpaan iyalputaiya moovarkkum,
Nallaatrin nindra thunai.
kurals.meaning: The one who truly deserves the name “householder” is the steady support, along the path of virtue, of the three others who depend on him.
kurals.elementary: Think of a family like a table. The person who runs the household is the tabletop — everyone else rests on it. Parents, partner, children (and in the old way of counting, students, hermits, and wandering monks) all lean on the householder, and a good householder holds them all up and keeps them going the right way.
kurals.university: The chapter that opens the இல்லறவியல் (illaraviyal, “the way of domestic virtue”) begins by defining the householder functionally rather than sentimentally: he is a துணை (thunai, “support/companion/prop”) who stands நல்லாற்றின் (nallaatrin, “in the good way”). Commentators split sharply on who the “three” (மூவர்) are. Parimelazhagar and the older Sanskritising tradition read them as the other three ashramas — brahmacharin, vanaprastha and sannyasin — aligning the verse with Manu's grihastha doctrine; Kalaignar Karunanidhi and Salomon Pappaiah read them domestically as parents, spouse and children (or children, parents and kin). Valluvar's deliberate vagueness lets both readings stand, which is characteristic of his non-sectarian method. The crucial word is நின்ற (nindra, “having stood firm”) — not occasional charity but a standing, load-bearing role, and the standing must be *on the right path*, so that support which enables wrongdoing does not count.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As all living creatures subsist by receiving support from air, even so (the members of) all orders subsist by receiving support from the householder.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu argues that the student, forest-hermit and renunciant orders cannot function at all without the householder's food and gifts, which is why he calls the householder's order the most excellent.
hinduism.tie_back: This is almost the same sentence as the Kural: the householder is the firm support of the other three orders.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 3.77 (Bühler, Sacred Books of the East XXV)
hinduism._accuracy_note: A near-identical doctrine expressed with the same three-other-orders structure; almost certainly the shared intellectual background of the Kural.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.”
christianity.explanation: Paul makes material provision for one's household not an optional kindness but the minimum test of genuine faith.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts define the householder by the duty of being a reliable support to dependents, and treat failure there as a failure of virtue itself.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close on the duty of support; the Kural adds the 'good path' qualifier and a wider circle of dependents than Paul's immediate household.

islam.quote_or_event: “All of you are guardians and responsible for your wards and the things under your care. The Imam (i.e. ruler) is the guardian of his subjects and is responsible for them and a man is the guardian of his family and is responsible for them.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet frames every social role as a trust (ra'iyyah) for which one will be held accountable, with the head of a household explicitly named.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the householder's accountable support of dependents the defining content of the role, not an extra.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 893, Book of Friday Prayer
islam._accuracy_note: Strong on responsibility-for-dependents; the hadith's frame is accountability before God rather than the Kural's 'standing on the good path'.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud enumerates the obligations a father owes a son — to circumcise him, redeem him, teach him Torah, marry him off, and teach him a trade (some add: teach him to swim) — treating the household head as legally bound to equip those in his care for life.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic law turns paternal affection into an enforceable list of duties, so that being a householder is a bundle of specific obligations rather than a status.
judaism.tie_back: Both traditions define the householder as one who is obligated to be a practical, ongoing support to those naturally dependent on him.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not a verified verbatim quotation; strong on duty-to-dependents but narrower (father-to-son) than the Kural's threefold circle.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigalovada Sutta the Buddha reinterprets the young householder Sigala's ritual worship of the six directions as the householder's reciprocal duties toward parents (east), teachers (south), wife and children (west), friends (north), workers (below) and ascetics and brahmins (above).
buddhism.explanation: The sutta is the classic Buddhist charter of lay life: the householder is the hub of a web of mutual obligations, including support of the renunciant community.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the householder the structural support of several distinct groups, explicitly including those who have renounced.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the sutta's well-known structure rather than a verified quotation; the six-directions scheme matches the Kural's logic closely but counts six groups, not three.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “First of all, get a house, and a woman and an ox for the plough … and make everything ready at home, so that you may not have to ask of another, and he refuses you, and so, because you are in lack, the season pass by and your work come to nothing.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod's farmer's almanac treats the establishment of a self-sufficient household as the first move in a virtuous life; the ellipsis omits his harsh qualification that the woman be a hired labourer rather than a wife.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both texts put the household first in the moral order, though Hesiod's emphasis is self-sufficiency where the Kural's is supporting others.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Honest next-best match: Hesiod grounds virtue in the household, but his point is not depending on others, which is nearly the inverse of the Kural's point about being depended upon.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Duties are universally measured by relations. Is anyone a father? If so, it is implied that the children should take care of him, submit to him in everything, patiently listen to his reproaches, his correction.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus derives concrete obligations directly from one's place in a web of relationships — father, brother, neighbour, citizen — rather than from abstract rules.
philosophy.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural's method: the householder's virtue is defined by the relations he stands in and what those relations require of him.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close in method (duties from relations); Epictetus stresses duties owed *to* the householder as much as by him.

kurals.tamil:
துறந்தார்க்கும் துவ்வாதவர்க்கும் இறந்தார்க்கும்
இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான் துணை.
kurals.transliteration:
Thurandhaarkkum thuvvaadhavarkkum irandhaarkkum,
Ilvaazhvaan enpaan thunai.
kurals.meaning: The householder is the support of those who have renounced the world, of those who have nothing to eat, and of those who have died.
kurals.elementary: Imagine one family in a village that keeps a pot of rice always ready. The travelling monk who owns nothing eats from it. The hungry neighbour eats from it. And a share is set aside in memory of grandparents who have died. That one household quietly feeds three groups who cannot feed themselves.
kurals.university: Valluvar names three classes with three neat participial nouns: துறந்தார் (thurandhaar, “those who have let go”), துவ்வாதவர் (thuvvaadhavar, literally “those who do not eat” — the destitute), and இறந்தார் (irandhaar, “those who have passed”). The last is the most striking to a modern reader: the dead are treated as an ongoing claim on the living, through the memorial offerings (தென்புலத்தார் rites) that the next couplet will name explicitly. The verse is a deliberate argumentative move within a Tamil intellectual landscape in which Jain and Buddhist renunciant ideals were culturally prestigious: Valluvar concedes the renunciant's standing and then points out that the renunciant literally eats because a householder cooked. Economic dependency becomes a moral argument for the dignity of domestic life.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Charity given out of duty, without expectation of return, at the proper time and place, and to a worthy person is considered to be in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna classifies charity by motive: sattvic giving is given because it ought to be given, to those who genuinely merit it, with no thought of return.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's householder gives to renunciants, the destitute and the dead — three classes that by definition can never repay him.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches well on non-reciprocal giving as the householder's duty, but the Gita does not enumerate the same three recipients.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.”
christianity.explanation: James relocates the essence of religion from ritual to the concrete care of society's most defenceless members.
christianity.tie_back: Both verses define true piety as practical support for those who cannot support themselves, rather than as withdrawal or ceremony.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close on care for the destitute; James has no counterpart to the Kural's duties toward renunciants or the dead.

islam.quote_or_event: “…but [true] righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets and gives wealth, in spite of love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler, those who ask [for help], and for freeing slaves…”
islam.explanation: The famous 'verse of righteousness' lists the specific categories of dependent people whose support constitutes real piety, against merely outward observance.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it measures a person's virtue by the list of unrepaying dependants he sustains out of his own household wealth.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong structural parallel (an enumerated list of dependants); the Qur'anic list omits the dead and renunciants, since Islam has no monastic order.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Charity is given to the living, while acts of kindness are performed both for the living and for the dead.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud ranks gemilut chasadim above tzedakah partly because kindness extends to the dead — burial and mourning rites are called chesed shel emet, 'true kindness', since the recipient can never repay.
judaism.tie_back: This is an unusually exact parallel: the Kural likewise lists the dead alongside the poor as recipients of the householder's support.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Sukkah 49b (Koren-Steinsaltz / William Davidson Edition)
judaism._accuracy_note: Extremely close on the distinctive point — duties owed to the dead as well as the living — from an authentically Jewish, not merely biblical, source.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Householders & the homeless / in mutual dependence / both reach the true Dhamma: / the unsurpassed safety from bondage. / From householders, the homeless / receive requisites: robes, lodgings, / protection from inclemencies.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the lay-monastic relationship as reciprocal: householders supply material requisites, monastics supply the Dhamma, and neither reaches the goal without the other.
buddhism.tie_back: This states the Kural's first clause outright — the renunciant (துறந்தார்) survives because the householder supports him.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on the householder-supports-the-renunciant claim, and from the tradition whose renunciant prestige Valluvar is implicitly answering.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Sophocles' Antigone, Antigone defies Creon's edict and performs burial rites for her brother Polyneices, insisting that the unwritten laws owed to the dead outrank a ruler's decree, and accepts death rather than leave him unburied.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek religion held that the dead had an enforceable claim on their kin for burial and grave offerings, and that failing them polluted the whole household and city.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It matches the Kural's most distinctive element — that the dead (இறந்தார்) remain dependants of the living household.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the plot rather than a verified quotation; it captures the duty-to-the-dead strand well but says nothing about renunciants or the poor.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero argues in De Officiis that we are not born for ourselves alone — our country, our parents, our friends and our fellow human beings each claim a share of our existence — and that this is why generosity and beneficence are duties of justice rather than optional favours.
philosophy.explanation: Stoic-influenced Roman ethics grounds the obligation to support others in the claim that a person's life is partly owned by the communities that made it possible.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts derive the householder's obligation to support non-reciprocating others from the simple fact of belonging to a community.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not a verified verbatim; the principle matches but Cicero's list of claimants is civic rather than the Kural's three specific classes.

kurals.tamil:
தென்புலத்தார் தெய்வம் விருந்தொக்கல் தானென்றாங்கு
ஐம்புலத்தாறு ஓம்பல் தலை.
kurals.transliteration:
Thenpulaththaar theyvam virundhokkal thaanendraangu,
Aimpulaththaaru ompal thalai.
kurals.meaning: The householder's foremost duty is to cherish, in due measure, five claims: the departed ancestors, the gods, guests, kinfolk, and oneself.
kurals.elementary: A good household is like a table set with five plates. One is for the grandparents who have passed away, one is for God, one for whoever knocks at the door, one for the family, and one for yourself. Forgetting any plate — including your own — means the table isn't really set.
kurals.university: This is the Kural's compressed version of the fivefold domestic obligation. தென்புலத்தார் (thenpulaththaar) literally means “those of the southern region” — the dead, since the south is Yama's quarter — and is the standard Tamil term for the ancestors (pitṛ). The other four are தெய்வம் (theyvam, the gods), விருந்து (virundhu, the guest — a theme Valluvar gives a whole chapter to at 9), ஒக்கல் (okkal, kin), and தான் (thaan, oneself). The inclusion of *oneself* is philosophically important: Valluvar's domestic ethic is not self-erasing asceticism but a balanced distribution, captured by ஓம்பல் (ombal, “to cherish/tend/guard”) and by தலை (thalai, “the head, the foremost thing”). The scheme corresponds closely to the Brahminical pañca-mahāyajña, but Valluvar strips it of ritual technicality and states it as household budgeting of love and resources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “But he who does not feed these five, the gods, his guests, those whom he is bound to maintain, the manes, and himself, lives not, though he breathes.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu's formulation of the five great sacrifices makes daily household life itself a continuous ritual obligation toward gods, guests, dependants, ancestors and self.
hinduism.tie_back: The five items and their order are effectively identical to the Kural's ஐம்புலம் — gods, guests, kin, the departed, and oneself.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 3.72 (Bühler, Sacred Books of the East XXV)
hinduism._accuracy_note: As close as cross-textual matches get: the same five categories, including the unusual inclusion of oneself.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews grounds Christian hospitality in the Genesis episode of Abraham unknowingly hosting divine messengers, making the guest a potential bearer of the sacred.
christianity.tie_back: It fuses two of the Kural's five claims — the guest (விருந்து) and the divine (தெய்வம்) — into a single duty of the household.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on the guest-and-god pairing but covers only two of the Kural's five obligations.

islam.quote_or_event: “Anybody who believes in Allah and the Last Day should not harm his neighbor, and anybody who believes in Allah and the Last Day should entertain his guest generously and anybody who believes in Allah and the Last Day should talk what is good or keep quiet.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet lists domestic and neighbourly conduct — not private devotion — as the direct proof of belief in God and the hereafter.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats honouring the guest and one's immediate circle as the householder's headline religious duty.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 6018, Book of Good Manners (Al-Adab)
islam._accuracy_note: Very strong on hospitality and neighbourly kin duty; no Islamic counterpart to offerings to ancestors, which is a real divergence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hospitality toward guests is greater than receiving the Divine Presence.”
judaism.explanation: Rav derives this from Abraham asking God to wait while he attends to three travellers (Genesis 18:3), making hachnasat orchim outrank even direct communion with God.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural lists guests alongside the gods among the five claims; the Talmud goes further and ranks the guest above the divine visitation.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 127a (Koren-Steinsaltz / William Davidson Edition)
judaism._accuracy_note: Excellent on the guest-versus-god ranking; like the Islamic parallel it lacks an ancestor-offering element.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “…performs the five oblations: to relatives, guests, the dead, kings, & devas. This is the fourth benefit that can be obtained from wealth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the householder Anathapindika that righteously earned wealth should be used for five purposes, one of which is a set of five customary offerings.
buddhism.tie_back: Four of the Kural's five claims appear verbatim here — relatives, guests, the dead, and the gods — as duties of household wealth.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.41, Adiya Sutta, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strikingly exact overlap of an enumerated fivefold list; the Buddhist list substitutes kings for 'oneself', which AN 5.41 covers in its first benefit instead.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid tells how Jupiter and Mercury, travelling disguised, are turned away by a thousand homes until the poor elderly couple Baucis and Philemon welcome them into their one-room cottage, share their scant food, and are spared the flood that destroys their impious neighbours.
greek_mythology.explanation: The tale is the definitive Greco-Roman statement of xenia — the sacred obligation of the household hearth to the stranger, enforced by Zeus Xenios himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatises three of the Kural's five claims at once: the guest, the gods, and the household itself, all met at a single hearth.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the narrative rather than a quotation; superb on guest-and-god but silent on kin, ancestors and self.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero maps the degrees of human fellowship in concentric circles and holds that the first bond of society is that between husband and wife, then parents and children, then the household — which he calls the foundation of civil government and, as it were, the nursery of the state.
philosophy.explanation: For Cicero, moral obligation is graded: we owe most to those nearest, and the household is the training ground from which civic duty grows.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts organise the householder's duties as a ranked set of claims radiating outward from the home.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified verbatim; the graded-obligation structure matches, but Cicero's list is civic rather than the Kural's ritual-domestic five.

kurals.tamil:
பழியஞ்சிப் பாத்தூண் உடைத்தாயின் வாழ்க்கை
வழியெஞ்சல் எஞ்ஞான்றும் இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pazhiyanjip paaththoon utaiththaayin vaazhkkai,
Vazhiyenjal egngnaandrum il.
kurals.meaning: If a household shuns blame in how it earns and shares out what it eats, its line will never fail, in any age.
kurals.elementary: Suppose a family grows apples honestly and always gives some away to neighbours. Everyone keeps trading with them, everyone helps them in a bad year, and the orchard keeps going for generations. A family that steals its apples and eats them alone soon has neither friends nor orchard.
kurals.university: Two conditions are compressed into one line: பழியஞ்சி (pazhi-anji, “fearing blame/reproach”) governs *acquisition*, and பாத்தூண் (paath-ūṇ, from பகுத்து உண்ணல், “eating after apportioning”) governs *consumption*. The reward is stated negatively and absolutely: வழி எஞ்சல் … இல் — “there is never a failing of the line.” வழி (vazhi) means both “way” and “lineage,” so the promise is simultaneously that the household's path and its descendants will not run out. Note that Valluvar's ethical lever here is பழி (pazhi, public blame) rather than sin — an honour-and-reproach vocabulary rooted in Tamil Sangam social ethics rather than in a theology of divine punishment, which is part of why the Kural reads as secular to modern audiences.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The devotees of the Lord are released from all kinds of sins because they eat food which is offered first for sacrifice. Others, who prepare food for personal sense enjoyment, verily eat only sin.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna contrasts food that has first been offered and shared with food cooked purely for one's own gratification, calling the latter itself a form of wrongdoing.
hinduism.tie_back: This is precisely the Kural's பாத்தூண் principle: eating only what has first been apportioned to others is what keeps the household clean.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close on shared-versus-selfish eating; the Gita frames the sharing as sacrificial offering rather than social distribution.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He hath dispersed abroad; he hath given to the poor: his righteousness remaineth for ever. Now he that ministereth seed to the sower both minister bread for your food, and multiply your seed sown, and increase the fruits of your righteousness.”
christianity.explanation: Paul uses an agricultural image: giving away is sowing, and the giver's store is replenished and multiplied rather than depleted.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts promise that the household which shares its food does not diminish but endures and multiplies.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on sharing-leads-to-increase; Paul does not address the 'fear of blame in acquiring' half of the couplet.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they give food in spite of love for it to the needy, the orphan, and the captive,”
islam.explanation: Surah al-Insan praises the righteous specifically for giving away food they themselves want, and promises them lasting reward.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural's second condition exactly — the household's virtue lies in apportioning its own meal outward.
islam._accuracy_note: Near-exact on sharing food despite wanting it; the promise of an unbroken lineage is not part of this verse.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I have been young, and now am old; yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread. He is ever merciful, and lendeth; and his seed is blessed.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist's lifelong observation is that generosity and descendants' security go together — the open-handed man's children do not end up beggars.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact promise: the household that shares its bread finds its line never fails.
judaism._accuracy_note: An unusually precise match on both halves — generosity and the unbroken, unbegging lineage.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Truly, misers fare not to heavenly realms; nor, indeed, do fools praise generosity. But the wise man rejoices in giving, and by that alone does he become happy hereafter.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada makes generosity the decisive factor in a layperson's future welfare, and hoarding the decisive obstacle.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts tie the household's long-term fortune directly to whether it shares what it has.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good on generosity-and-future-good; the Buddhist reward is a personal heavenly rebirth rather than the Kural's continuing family line.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Wealth should not be seized: god-given wealth is much better; for it a man take great wealth violently and perforce, or if he steal it through his tongue … the gods soon blot him out and make that man's house low, and wealth attends him only for a little time.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns his brother Perses that dishonestly gotten wealth is punished by Zeus not just personally but at the level of the household, which is brought low.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's first condition stated as its negative: the household that does not fear blame in acquiring will see its line fail.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very close on blameless acquisition determining the survival of the house; Hesiod does not pair it with the sharing of food.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle analyses liberality (eleutheriotes) as a mean concerning wealth: the liberal person gives the right amounts to the right people at the right time, gives from his own resources rather than by taking wrongly, and cares more about giving well than about getting.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle the virtue is not generosity alone but the pairing of clean acquisition with well-judged distribution — the two are aspects of a single disposition.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural makes exactly that pairing: blameless earning and apportioned eating are two halves of one household virtue.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Aristotle's analysis rather than a verified quotation; the earn-cleanly-and-share-well pairing matches well, but Aristotle promises no generational outcome.

kurals.tamil:
அன்பும் அறனும் உடைத்தாயின் இல்வாழ்க்கை
பண்பும் பயனும் அது.
kurals.transliteration:
Anpum aranum utaiththaayin ilvaazhkkai,
Panpum payanum adhu.
kurals.meaning: If domestic life possesses love and virtue, then that possession is at once its true character and its whole reward.
kurals.elementary: Think of a fruit tree that is both beautiful and gives fruit. You don't grow it for some other prize somewhere else — the tree being what it is *is* the prize. A home with love and goodness in it is the same: it is not a step toward the good life, it already is the good life.
kurals.university: The verse turns on a deliberate identity statement: பண்பும் பயனும் அது — “its quality and its fruit are *that*.” Valluvar collapses the usual ethical distinction between a virtue and the reward the virtue earns. அன்பு (anpu, love) and அறன் (aran, virtue/dharma) are not instruments for obtaining household happiness; they *constitute* it. This is a genuinely Aristotelian move — the household, rightly constituted, is an end in itself, not a means — and it is what allows Valluvar in the following verses to argue that the householder need not look elsewhere (46) and outranks the ascetic (48). அன்பு gets a full chapter later (8, அன்புடைமை); here it is paired with அறன் so that affection alone is not enough, nor correctness alone.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “In that family, where the husband is pleased with his wife and the wife with her husband, happiness will assuredly be lasting.”
hinduism.explanation: Amid a chapter of ritual prescriptions, Manu states plainly that mutual delight between spouses is the condition of a household's durable well-being.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts locate the household's happiness in the quality of affection inside it rather than in any external result.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 3.60 (Bühler, Sacred Books of the East XXV)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close on love-as-the-source-of-household-good; Manu speaks only of the spousal pair, not of virtue alongside love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness.”
christianity.explanation: Writing to a household-based congregation, Paul lists the virtues and then names love as the binding agent that holds them together and completes them.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural makes the same claim structurally: love plus virtue is not a route to completeness but is the completeness itself.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on love-as-completion; Paul's frame is the Christian community, which includes but is not limited to the household.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of His signs is that He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquillity in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy. Indeed in that are signs for a people who give thought.”
islam.explanation: Marriage is presented as a sign of God, its purpose being sakīnah (tranquillity), with mawaddah (affection) and raḥmah (mercy) placed between the couple.
islam.tie_back: Affection and mercy are named as the constituents of married life exactly as அன்பு and அறன் are in the Kural, and the tranquillity is the state itself, not a later payoff.
islam._accuracy_note: Outstanding match: a two-term pairing of love and moral kindness as the defining content of domestic life.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs weighs a household's material abundance against its emotional quality and decides unambiguously for love.
judaism.tie_back: Both couplets say that the household's worth lies in the love inside it, not in what the household yields.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close in sentiment and in the domestic-meal setting; Proverbs contrasts love with wealth rather than pairing love with virtue.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If both husband & wife want to see one another not only in the present life but also in the life to come, they should be in tune [with each other] in conviction, in tune in virtue, in tune in generosity, and in tune in discernment.”
buddhism.explanation: Answering the devoted couple Nakulapita and Nakulamata, the Buddha says that a marriage endures on shared moral qualities, not on feeling alone.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it insists on the pairing: affection must be matched by shared virtue for domestic life to be what it should be.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.55, Samajivina Sutta, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very strong on love-plus-virtue as the substance of married life; the sutta's payoff is future rebirth together, slightly unlike the Kural's 'the reward is the thing itself'.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “May heaven grant you in all things your heart's desire — husband, house, and a happy, peaceful home; for there is nothing better in this world than that man and wife should be of one mind in a house. It discomfits their enemies, makes the hearts of their friends glad, and they themselves know more about it than any one.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus, shipwrecked and naked, blesses Nausicaa with the highest good he can name: homophrosynē, the like-mindedness of husband and wife.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim in Homeric form — that a household of shared mind and heart is simply the best thing there is, not a means to something better.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: An exceptionally close parallel — 'there is nothing better in this world' is functionally identical to 'its quality and its fruit are that'.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that the friendship between husband and wife exists by nature, combines the useful and the pleasant, and becomes best of all when the partners are good, so that each delights in the other's virtue; on that basis children too are a bond.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle the highest form of philia is between good people who love each other for their virtue, and he explicitly applies this to marriage.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact combination — love and virtue together — as what makes a household both what it ought to be and worth having.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase rather than a verified verbatim quotation, but the conceptual match — virtue-based spousal friendship as an end in itself — is very strong.

kurals.tamil:
அறத்தாற்றின் இல்வாழ்க்கை ஆற்றின் புறத்தாற்றில்
போஒய்ப் பெறுவ தெவன்?
kurals.transliteration:
Araththaatrin ilvaazhkkai aatrin puraththaatril,
Pooip peruva thevan?
kurals.meaning: If a person conducts domestic life along the path of virtue, what more is there to be gained by going off to some other path?
kurals.elementary: If the water in your own well is clean and cold, why walk ten miles to another village's well? The answer is: there's no reason to. Living well at home already gives you what you would go looking for elsewhere.
kurals.university: The couplet is framed as a rhetorical question — பெறுவது எவன்? (“what is there to obtain?”) — and the expected answer is “nothing.” புறத்தாற்றில் (puraththaatril, “on the outside path”) is the polite euphemism for the ascetic's road, the துறவறம் that Valluvar treats sympathetically in chapters 3 and 35. The argument is not that renunciation is false but that it is redundant *for someone already doing the domestic path properly*, the operative qualifier being அறத்தாற்றின் (“by the way of virtue”). Note the doubled ஆறு/ஆற்று root — path, path, outside-path — which makes the verse a small meditation on the metaphor of the road itself. This is the pivot on which the whole chapter, and arguably the whole of Book I's householder section, turns.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is unattached to the fruits of his work and who works as he is obligated is in the renounced order of life, and he is the true mystic, not he who lights no fire and performs no duty.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna redefines sannyāsa as an inner condition available to anyone doing their duty, explicitly denying that extinguishing the household fire makes one a renunciant.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's argument almost verbatim: the household path rightly followed already contains whatever the outside path was supposed to supply.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Outstanding match — both texts deflate the prestige of formal renunciation in favour of duty performed in place.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils; … Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth.”
christianity.explanation: The Pastoral Epistles attack an early ascetic movement that treated marriage and food as impediments to holiness, calling the doctrine demonic.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts push back against the assumption that leaving domestic life is a higher spiritual road.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong anti-ascetic parallel; the epistle condemns compulsory celibacy outright where the Kural merely calls the ascetic path superfluous.

islam.quote_or_event: “Are you the same people who said so-and-so? By Allah, I am more submissive to Allah and more afraid of Him than you; yet I fast and break my fast, I do sleep and I also marry women. So he who does not follow my tradition in religion, is not from me.”
islam.explanation: Three men had resolved to pray all night, fast perpetually, and never marry; the Prophet rebuked them, making moderate married life the normative religious path.
islam.tie_back: It answers the Kural's rhetorical question with a flat 'nothing' — there is no superior road outside the ordinary married life.
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: the same argument, the same target, and the same preference for the householder's path.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud records Rabbi Elazar HaKappar's view that the nazirite who abstains from wine must bring a sin-offering because he denied himself something permitted, and that anyone who afflicts himself by further such abstentions is called a sinner.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic Judaism is structurally suspicious of voluntary self-denial: creation's permitted pleasures are to be sanctified in ordinary life, not renounced.
judaism.tie_back: Both traditions deny that stepping outside ordinary domestic life earns any additional merit.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the sugya rather than a verified verbatim; the anti-ascetic stance matches strongly, though Judaism's target is self-denial rather than a rival monastic institution.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Neither going about naked, nor matted locks, nor filth, nor fasting, nor lying on the ground, nor smearing oneself with ashes and dust, nor sitting on the heels (in penance) can purify a mortal who has not overcome doubt.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha, who had himself tried extreme austerity, denies that any external ascetic practice purifies anyone by itself.
buddhism.tie_back: It grants the Kural's premise that the outside path holds no automatic advantage, though it does not go on to prefer the householder.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Honest partial match: Buddhism deflates *external* asceticism but still ranks the homeless life above the household, which is the opposite of the Kural's implication.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Held for seven years on Ogygia by the goddess Calypso, who offers to make him immortal and ageless if he stays as her husband, Odysseus refuses and weeps on the shore, choosing his mortal wife Penelope and his house on Ithaca over deathlessness.
greek_mythology.explanation: The episode is Greek epic's sharpest statement that domestic life with mortal kin is worth more than a transcendent condition outside it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Odysseus answers the Kural's question in narrative form: even godhood on another path is not worth leaving a rightly ordered home.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the episode rather than a quotation; the choice-of-home-over-transcendence is a genuinely strong echo, though Odysseus's motive is longing rather than ethical argument.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “he who is unable to live in society, or who has no need because he is sufficient for himself, must be either a beast or a god”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle holds that human flourishing is constitutively social, beginning in the household; the solitary self-sufficient life is not a higher human option but a non-human one.
philosophy.tie_back: Both deny that stepping outside the household and its bonds leads anywhere better for a human being.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on the impossibility of a superior solitary path; Aristotle's target is the apolitical individual rather than the religious ascetic specifically.

kurals.tamil:
இயல்பினான் இல்வாழ்க்கை வாழ்பவன் என்பான்
முயல்வாருள் எல்லாம் தலை.
kurals.transliteration:
Iyalpinaan ilvaazhkkai vaazhpavan enpaan,
Muyalvaarul ellaam thalai.
kurals.meaning: The one who lives domestic life according to its proper nature stands at the head of all who strive for the good.
kurals.elementary: In a race, lots of people train in fancy ways. But the one who simply runs correctly, step after step, finishes first. The person who does ordinary family life properly is that runner — ahead of everyone who is trying harder in more dramatic ways.
kurals.university: The decisive word is இயல்பினான் (iyalpinaan) — “by [its] nature,” the same root as இயல்புடைய in kural 41. Valluvar is not praising domestic life as such but domestic life lived *according to what it intrinsically is*, which chapters 41-46 have just specified: support of dependants, the fivefold obligation, blameless earning, shared food, love and virtue. Against that, முயல்வாருள் எல்லாம் தலை — “the head of all who exert themselves” — uses முயல் (muyal, to strive/labour), a word that in the religious register covers ascetic exertion and spiritual practice. The claim is competitive and startling for its time: the householder is not merely an acceptable alternative to the striving religious, he outranks them. Parimelazhagar's commentary reads this as Valluvar explicitly ranking இல்லறம் above துறவறம்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And in accordance with the precepts of the Veda and of the Smriti, the housekeeper is declared to be superior to all of them; for he supports the other three.”
hinduism.explanation: Having described the student, hermit and ascetic orders at length, Manu concludes by ranking the householder above all of them on the ground that he sustains them.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact claim — the householder is the head of all who strive — and with the same supporting reason.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 6.89 (Bühler, Sacred Books of the East XXV)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Essentially the same sentence: householder ranked first among the recognised religious modes of life.

christianity.quote_or_event: “One that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity; (For if a man know not how to rule his own house, how shall he take care of the church of God?)”
christianity.explanation: The qualification for the highest office in the early church is not ascetic achievement but demonstrated competence as a householder.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts treat well-run domestic life as the benchmark against which other forms of religious striving are measured.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong: household competence as the qualifying credential; the epistle makes it a prerequisite for leadership rather than the highest state in itself.

islam.quote_or_event: “The best of you is the best to his wives, and I am the best of you to my wives, and when your companion dies, leave him alone.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet locates the measure of a person's excellence squarely in domestic conduct, and names himself as the example.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes 'best of all' a ranking decided inside the home rather than by any extraordinary religious exertion.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close on domestic conduct as the criterion of being foremost; the hadith narrows the field to treatment of one's wife.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that a man without a wife lives without joy, without blessing and without goodness, and in the surrounding discussion treats marriage and the household as the normal setting in which a Jew fulfils his obligations.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic culture made the married scholar, not the celibate ascetic, the ideal type; an unmarried man was considered incomplete for religious as well as social purposes.
judaism.tie_back: Both traditions put the householder, not the solitary religious striver, at the top of the scale.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage rather than a verified verbatim quotation; the householder-as-ideal match is strong.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Instructing the layman Dighajanu, who says he cannot live as a renunciant, the Buddha lays out four conditions for welfare in this life — persistent effort, protecting what one earns, good friendship, and balanced livelihood — and four for the life to come, treating lay life as a complete and honourable path.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha gives householders a full curriculum rather than a consolation prize, though the monastic life remains the higher road in the Theravada scheme.
buddhism.tie_back: It affirms the Kural's respect for the striving householder without going as far as ranking him first.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Honest weak match, given as a paraphrase: Buddhism dignifies lay life but explicitly does not place the householder at the head of all who strive.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “So Zeus the Father gave her an high honour instead of marriage, and she has her place in the midst of the house and has the richest portion. In all the temples of the gods she has a share of honour, and among all mortal men she is chief of the goddesses.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hestia, goddess of the hearth at the centre of every Greek house, received the first portion of every sacrifice; the household fire was literally the first claim in Greek worship.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Greek cult makes the household hearth the foremost object of honour, as the Kural makes the householder foremost among all who strive.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Genuine parallel on the primacy of the hearth in religious ranking, but it honours a goddess of the household rather than the human householder, and Hestia is notably unmarried.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Remember that you are an actor in a drama, of such a kind as the author pleases to make it. If short, of a short one; if long, of a long one. … For this is your business, to act well the character assigned you; to choose it is another's.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus insists that excellence consists in performing well the role one actually has, not in acquiring a grander role.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's இயல்பினான் says the same: greatness comes from living domestic life according to its own proper nature, not from trading it for a loftier path.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Excellent on the 'live your assigned role according to its nature' principle; Epictetus does not rank roles against each other as the Kural does.

kurals.tamil:
ஆற்றின் ஒழுக்கி அறனிழுக்கா இல்வாழ்க்கை
நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Aatrin ozhukki aranizhukkaa ilvaazhkkai,
Norpaarin nonmai utaiththu.
kurals.meaning: A domestic life that keeps others moving along the right path and never itself slips from virtue has greater strength than the austerities of those who do penance.
kurals.elementary: One person sits alone on a hill and eats nothing for a week — that's hard. Another person gets up every day, stays honest, feeds the family, and gently keeps everyone else honest too — for fifty years. This kural says the second one is doing the harder, stronger thing.
kurals.university: The verse builds a careful two-part condition before making its comparison. ஆற்றின் ஒழுக்கி (aatrin ozhukki) is causative — “having caused [others] to conduct themselves on the path” — while அறனிழுக்கா (aran-izhukkaa) is negative and reflexive: “not itself slipping from virtue.” Only a household meeting both conditions is then said to possess நோன்மை (nonmai) exceeding that of நோற்பார் (norpaar, those who undertake நோன்பு, austerity/penance). The pun is the point: நோன்மை means both “endurance under penance” and “strength,” so Valluvar claims the householder wins the ascetic's own contest on the ascetic's own metric. This is the chapter's most polemical line and reflects a broader Tamil bhakti-era and post-Sangam argument against Jain and Buddhist monastic prestige.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Whatever action a great man performs, common men follow. And whatever standards he sets by exemplary acts, all the world pursues.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna cites the householder-king Janaka, who attained perfection through action, to argue that a person of standing must keep working precisely in order to guide others by example.
hinduism.tie_back: This supplies the Kural's first condition exactly — the householder's virtue is measured by his capacity to keep others on the path.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very strong: Janaka is Hinduism's canonical case of an active householder surpassing renunciants, and the verse states the guide-others principle directly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus places the moral value of visible, ordinary good conduct in its effect on others, immediately after warning against hiding a lamp under a bushel.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts make guiding others by one's own consistent conduct the measure of a life, rather than private feats of self-denial.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good on lead-others-by-example; the Gospel does not make the comparison with ascetic practice that gives the Kural its edge.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones, over which are [appointed] angels, harsh and severe…”
islam.explanation: The verse is traditionally read as commanding the head of a household to instruct and morally safeguard his dependants, not merely himself.
islam.tie_back: It matches the Kural's dual condition precisely: keep yourself from slipping and keep your household on the right path.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close on the self-and-others double duty of the householder; the Qur'anic frame is eschatological rather than a strength contest with ascetics.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.”
judaism.explanation: The Shema makes the ordinary rhythms of household life — sitting, walking, lying down, rising — the setting for transmitting the commandments to the next generation.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's ஆற்றின் ஒழுக்கி in practice: the household is where others are actually steered onto the right path.
judaism._accuracy_note: Excellent on the household as the engine of moral instruction, and it is a foundational Jewish text rather than an incidental proof-text.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One should first establish oneself in what is proper; then only should one instruct others. Thus the wise man will not be reproached.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada's self-chapter insists on the order of operations: self-correction precedes the correction of others, or the teaching is worthless.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural states the same two requirements in the same order — not slipping oneself, and guiding others along the path.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near-exact on the two-condition structure; the verse is addressed to anyone rather than specifically to householders.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “To you, foolish Perses, I will speak good sense. Badness can be got easily and in shoals: the road to her is smooth, and she lives very near us. But between us and Goodness the gods have placed the sweat of our brows: long and steep is the path that leads to her, and it is rough at the first.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Works and Days is framed as a farmer-householder correcting his idle brother, arguing that ordinary honest labour is the long steep road to virtue.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod's householder both walks the hard path himself and works to pull a wayward kinsman onto it — the Kural's two conditions in a single poem.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on the householder as moral instructor of his kin and on virtue as arduous; Hesiod never compares this to ascetic penance.

philosophy.quote_or_event: The Stoic Musonius Rufus argued in his lectures that marriage is no handicap to philosophy, that the philosopher must marry and raise children, and that the shared household is itself the arena in which self-control, justice and endurance are actually practised.
philosophy.explanation: Against the Cynic model of the unencumbered sage, Musonius insisted that the demands of spouse, children and household are harder training in virtue than solitude.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim in Roman Stoic form: domestic life possesses more real endurance than the withdrawn ascetic's regimen.
philosophy.source: Musonius Rufus, Lecture XIV, 'Is Marriage a Handicap for the Pursuit of Philosophy?'
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the lecture's argument rather than a verified verbatim quotation, but it is probably the closest philosophical analogue to this Kural in the entire Western tradition.

kurals.tamil:
அறனெனப் பட்டதே இல்வாழ்க்கை அஃதும்
பிறன்பழிப்ப தில்லாயின் நன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Aran enap pattadhe ilvaazhkkai aqdhum,
Piranpazhippa thillaayin nandru.
kurals.meaning: What has properly been called virtue is domestic life itself; and the other way of life too is good, provided no one has cause to reproach it.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone asks, "What does 'being good' actually mean?" This kural answers: it means running a home well. And it adds, politely, that the other way — going off to be a monk — is fine too, as long as nobody can point at it and say something is wrong.
kurals.university: The emphatic particle in அறனெனப் பட்டதே (aran-enap-pattadhē, “the very thing that has been called virtue”) is a definitional claim: domestic life is not *a* form of aram, it is what the word names. The second half is one of the Kural's most gracious sentences — அஃதும் (“that too”) concedes the ascetic path, but hedges it with a condition (பிறன் பழிப்பது இல்லாயின், “if there is nothing for another to reproach”) that Valluvar never attaches to the householder. Commentators differ over whether அஃதும் refers to the renunciant life or to a second grade of domestic life; the majority reading, followed by Mu. Varadarajan and Salomon Pappaiah, takes it as the ascetic path. Note the recurrence of பழி (pazhi, blame) from kural 44 — reproachability is Valluvar's working test for ethical failure throughout this chapter.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “As all rivers, both great and small, find a resting-place in the ocean, even so men of all orders find protection with householders.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu's closing image of the ashrama system makes the householder the ocean into which every other way of life eventually drains for support.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts make domestic life the substantive centre of dharma, with the other paths defined in relation to it.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 6.90 (Bühler, Sacred Books of the East XXV)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close on the household as the defining centre of religious life; Manu's image is about material support rather than a definition of virtue.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews affirms the moral standing of marriage without qualification, while attaching the reproach to its abuse rather than to the institution.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it declares married domestic life honourable in itself and locates blame only where conduct is actually faulty.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on marriage as honourable per se; the epistle does not take up the comparison with celibate life that the Kural's second clause handles.

islam.quote_or_event: “…And We placed in the hearts of those who followed him compassion and mercy and monasticism, which they innovated; We did not prescribe it for them except [that they did so] seeking the approval of Allah. But they did not observe it with due observance.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an treats Christian monasticism as a human innovation God never commanded, and notes that those who adopted it largely failed to keep it properly.
islam.tie_back: This is an almost eerie match for the Kural's second clause: the other path is conceded as possibly good, but only if it is actually kept without reproach.
islam._accuracy_note: Remarkably close on the conditional, slightly sceptical concession to the ascetic path — the same rhetorical shape as அஃதும் … நன்று.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And the LORD God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him.”
judaism.explanation: The first thing declared 'not good' in the Hebrew Bible is solitude, and the remedy is a partner — establishing companionate household life as the created norm.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's definition of virtue as domestic life has its scriptural counterpart here, where paired household existence is what God calls good.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on domestic partnership as the normative good; it is a creation statement rather than a definition of virtue, and says nothing about a rival path.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There are these four kinds of bliss that can be attained … by a householder … The bliss of having, the bliss of [making use of] wealth, the bliss of debtlessness, the bliss of blamelessness. … these are not worth one sixteenth-sixteenth of the bliss of blamelessness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Anathapindika that of everything a householder can enjoy, the incomparably greatest is anavajja-sukha, the happiness of being beyond reproach.
buddhism.tie_back: Blamelessness is exactly the test the Kural applies — the standard by which a way of life is judged good.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.62, Anana Sutta, trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu
buddhism._accuracy_note: Excellent on the blamelessness criterion applied specifically to householders; the sutta does not equate household life with virtue as such.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Iliad VI, Hector leaves the battlefield to find Andromache and their infant son Astyanax at the Scaean Gate; he removes his terrifying helmet so the baby will not cry, prays for the child's future, and tells his weeping wife that he fights precisely so that this household may stand.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer's most tender domestic scene sits deliberately inside a war poem, presenting the household as the good that all the heroism is ultimately for.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It implicitly makes the Kural's claim — that domestic life is the substantive good — though by dramatisation rather than definition.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Honest weak match, given as a paraphrase: it honours domestic life beautifully but never calls it virtue, and Greek epic has no ascetic alternative to weigh it against.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “the family is the association established by nature for the supply of men's everyday wants”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle begins the Politics by deriving every larger association from the household, which he treats as natural and prior rather than as a compromise or a lower stage.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts make the household the primary and defining human association rather than a preliminary to something higher.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good on the primacy and naturalness of the household; Aristotle's interest is political genealogy rather than the Kural's identification of household life with virtue itself.

kurals.tamil:
வையத்துள் வாழ்வாங்கு வாழ்பவன் வான்உறையும்
தெய்வத்துள் வைக்கப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vaiyaththul vaazhvaangu vaazhpavan vaanuraiyum,
Theyvaththul vaikkap padum.
kurals.meaning: Whoever lives on this earth in the way one ought to live will be reckoned among the gods who dwell in the sky.
kurals.elementary: You don't have to go anywhere special to become great. If you live rightly here — kindly, honestly, taking care of people — the world will think of you the way it thinks of the shining beings in the sky. Being good on the ground is what puts you up there.
kurals.university: The chapter's closing couplet is built on a deliberate spatial contrast: வையத்துள் (vaiyaththul, “within the world/earth”) against வான் உறையும் (vaan uraiyum, “sky-dwelling”). The pivot is the untranslatable வாழ்வாங்கு வாழ்பவன் — “one who lives in the manner of living,” i.e. one who lives as living is properly done. The passive வைக்கப்படும் (vaikkap-padum, “will be placed/reckoned”) is carefully non-supernatural: Valluvar does not say such a person *becomes* a god or *goes* to heaven, but that he will be *counted among* them — an evaluative rather than metaphysical claim, which is why the verse has been read comfortably by Saiva, Vaishnava, Jain and secular-humanist commentators alike. It is also the structural answer to kural 1: the book opened by putting God first; it closes this chapter by putting the good householder alongside the gods.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, the sage Kaushika, proud of his ascetic powers, is sent to learn dharma from Dharmavyadha — a butcher in Mithila who supports his aged parents and does his ordinary trade honestly; the householder-butcher then instructs the brahmin ascetic in the highest teaching.
hinduism.explanation: The Vyadha Gita makes an ordinary working householder the spiritual superior of a forest ascetic, precisely because he lives his worldly duties as they ought to be lived.
hinduism.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural's claim that living rightly in this world is what places a person among the highest, above those who chase higher states.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Vyadha Gita / the story of Dharmavyadha)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the narrative rather than a quotation; extremely close in message, though it ranks the householder above ascetics rather than literally among the gods.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whereby are given unto us exceeding great and precious promises: that by these ye might be partakers of the divine nature, having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust.”
christianity.explanation: 2 Peter articulates what the Eastern churches call theosis — that human beings living rightly come to share in God's own nature.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's promise in Christian terms: right living on earth results in being counted with the divine.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on divinisation through right living; the epistle attributes it to divine promise and grace rather than to domestic conduct as such.

islam.quote_or_event: “[To the righteous it will be said], 'O reassured soul, Return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing [to Him], And enter among My [righteous] servants And enter My Paradise.'”
islam.explanation: Surah al-Fajr closes by contrasting the greedy who neglect the orphan and the poor with the soul at peace, who is welcomed into the ranks of God's servants.
islam.tie_back: Both passages describe the reward as being *placed among* an honoured company — the Kural among the sky-dwelling gods, the Qur'an among God's servants.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close on the 'enter among' formula and on its being earned by earthly conduct toward dependants; Islam would not say a human is reckoned among gods.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Jacob said: this world is like a vestibule before the world to come; prepare yourself in the vestibule, so that you may enter the banqueting-hall.”
judaism.explanation: Pirkei Avot makes present, ordinary life the preparation whose quality determines one's place in the world to come.
judaism.tie_back: Both sayings make how one lives here the sole determinant of the honoured company one joins hereafter.
judaism.source: Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 4:16 (trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp)
judaism._accuracy_note: Good on earthly living determining a higher station; the Mishnah treats this world as preparatory where the Kural treats living rightly here as already the achievement.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Living with Brahma are those families where, in the home, mother & father are revered by the children. Living with the first devas are those families where, in the home, mother & father are revered by the children. … 'Brahma' is a designation for mother & father.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha says that a household which honours its parents is already living in the company of Brahma and the devas — and that the parents themselves *are* what those words name.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim almost exactly: rightly ordered domestic life places ordinary people among the gods.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Outstanding: the same identification of good householders with divine beings, and the closing verse adds that such people 'after death rejoice in heaven'.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But after earth had covered this generation -- they are called pure spirits dwelling on the earth, and are kindly, delivering from harm, and guardians of mortal men; for they roam everywhere over the earth, clothed in mist and keep watch on judgements and cruel deeds, givers of wealth”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod's golden race, who had lived rightly and died gently, were not simply extinguished but promoted to the status of daimones who guard and watch over the living.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says that mortals who lived as one ought are afterwards reckoned among the divine order rather than merely remembered.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong on right-living mortals joining the divine ranks; Hesiod's golden race qualify by belonging to a lost age rather than by individual household virtue.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Wherefore we ought to fly away from earth to heaven as quickly as we can; and to fly away is to become like God, as far as this is possible; and to become like him, is to become holy, just, and wise.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates defines the philosopher's goal as homoiōsis theōi — likeness to God — and immediately glosses it in purely ethical terms: holiness, justice, wisdom.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural makes the same move, defining nearness to the divine as a matter of how one lives rather than where one goes.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close on becoming godlike through right conduct; Plato's 'fly away from earth' is more world-renouncing than the Kural's insistence on living well *within* the world.
